::: {.part}
Part three · when pain stays
:::

## The system turns its own gain up {#gain .stop data-stop="gain"}

::: {.year}
2011
:::

::: {.lead}
Pain that goes on for months is often not a longer version of pain that lasts a week. The
equipment doing the measuring has changed its settings.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Woolf, 2011 [@woolf11] — a review by the person who named the phenomenon, in a supplement
issue of *Pain* devoted to it.

Well established as something that happens: it can be produced deliberately in volunteers,
and it shows up in brain recordings as well as in what people report. Much less settled is
how much of any one person's ongoing pain it accounts for — that step is inference, and it
is argued over. Treat "central sensitisation" as a described phenomenon, not as a diagnosis
you can make with your hands.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="gain"}
A schematic, not a measured curve from anybody. Drag the slider and watch a firm press
cross into pain without the press changing. The dashed line is the same nervous system
before.
:::

The technical name is
**[central sensitisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_sensitization){.wiki}**, and
the plain version is that a nervous system carrying pain signals for long enough can become
better at carrying them. The junction from part one gets more excitable. Less input is
needed to produce a signal, and the same input produces more.

Two consequences a practitioner meets constantly. Things that should not hurt begin to —
clothing, a light hand, a breeze. And things that should hurt a little hurt a lot. Neither
is exaggeration, and neither is a sign that the tissue got worse. The curve moved.

This is genuinely good news badly delivered. A system that has turned its gain up is
describing a settings change rather than more damage, and settings can change back. But
notice how carefully that has to be said: **the phenomenon is well described, and reading
it off any individual is not.** There is no test you can do in a treatment room that
establishes it, and a confident diagnosis of it from a practitioner is going beyond what
anyone can currently support.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
If pressure that never used to hurt now does, the useful first thought is *the system is
reading loudly*, not *I found the damaged bit*. It changes how hard you work, and it
changes what you say about what you found.
:::

## How much of it is the room {#room .stop data-stop="room"}

::: {.year}
2018
:::

::: {.lead}
Everything that arrives with a treatment — the words, the confidence, the setting, the
expectation — travels with it into the result, and some of it is doing more work than the
technique.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Rossettini, Carlino & Testa, 2018 [@rossettini18], written for musculoskeletal practitioners
and about their working conditions specifically.

A narrative review and a framework — **not data, and never to be cited as an effect size**.
Its value is in naming the things, not in measuring them. The measured demonstration that
context changes pain is the previous stop; this is the vocabulary for where it enters a
treatment room.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="room"}
The review's four categories, in plain words. Nothing here carries a number, because the
source does not have one — it is a map of what is in the room, not a measurement of what
each part does.
:::

The uncomfortable half of this is the **[nocebo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocebo){.wiki}**
side: the same channel runs in both directions. A phrase like *your pelvis is out*, *this is
the worst back I have seen today*, or *you should be careful with that forever* is not a
neutral description. It is an input to the system in the previous stop.

The comfortable half is that a practitioner has more legitimate influence here than the
sceptical version of this story allows. Being unhurried, being believed, being touched by
someone who seems to know what they are doing — these are not the parts of the treatment to
apologise for. They are part of the treatment.

What would be dishonest is to run this the other way and conclude that technique does not
matter, or that it is all in the telling. Nothing here shows that. It shows that the
telling is not free.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
The sentence a client repeats to their family that evening is part of what you did. Worth
choosing it as deliberately as you choose where to put your hands.
:::
